ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

A point of no return

A segment of tissue is exposed to prolonged ischemia in the laboratory. After oxygen and glucose are restored, some cells still cannot regenerate ATP and show extensive plasma-membrane disruption. Which interpretation best distinguishes these cells from reversibly injured cells?

  1. The cells show uncomplicated physiologic adaptation
  2. The changes establish reversible hydropic swelling only
  3. The cells are undergoing normal hyperplasia
  4. The restored circulation guarantees recovery
  5. The cells have sustained irreversible injury
Answer and explanation

The cells have sustained irreversible injury

Failure to recover mitochondrial function together with severe membrane damage supports irreversible injury.

Option explanations

The cells have sustained irreversible injury: Failure to recover mitochondrial function together with severe membrane damage supports irreversible injury.

The cells show uncomplicated physiologic adaptation: Adaptation preserves viability and does not explain catastrophic membrane loss.

The changes establish reversible hydropic swelling only: Simple swelling can reverse when energy supply returns; these cells cannot restore ATP.

The cells are undergoing normal hyperplasia: Hyperplasia increases viable cell number rather than disrupting membranes.

The restored circulation guarantees recovery: Reperfusion cannot rescue cells already irreversibly injured.
